newsitem.title: CANADA: Retrial likely in Canadian "mercy-killing" case.
newsitem.headline: Retrial likely in Canadian "mercy-killing" case.

text.p: The Supreme Court took under advisement on Wednesday a request by lawyers from both sides for a new trial for Robert Latimer, who has become a lightning rod in the mercy-killing debate in Canada.
The high court reserved decision on Latimer's appeal of his 1994 conviction of murdering his severely disabled 12-year-old daughter.
Both his lawyer Mark Brayford and prosecutor Carol Snell conceded there should be a new trial because of jury tampering in the original proceedings.
"Both parties to the appeal are at a minimum recommending that there be a new trial," Brayford told Reuters.
It was learned one year after Latimer's conviction that police questioned potential jurors about their views on euthanasia, abortion and religion prior to the trial.
Some of those questioned served on the jury.
The Saskatchewan farmer came to national prominence in 1993 after he said he killed his daughter Tracy to end her suffering.
Tracy -- who had the most severe form of cerebral palsy -- was a quadriplegic and could not walk, talk or feed herself. She died of carbon monoxide poisoning in October 1993.
Ten days after her death, Latimer told police he killed his daughter by placing her in his truck and running a hose from the truck's exhaust pipe to the cab where she sat.

Latimer was convicted of second-degree murder and given a life sentence with no chance of parole for 10 years. He has been out on bail during the lengthy appeal process and has spent only one day in jail since his conviction.
The case is an emotional one, but the ethical arguments were not the ones presented to the Supreme Court on Wednesday.

In addition to the jury tampering, Brayford argued to the top court that his client's constitutional rights were violated because police questioned him without placing him under formal arrest. He also said police did not advise Latimer that free legal advice was available.
One of the questions before the court was if his confession was excluded whether this would be grounds for acquittal.
The court's nine judges did not set a date for a decision.
People on both sides of the mercy-killing debate said the real issues risked being forgotten in all the legal wrangling.
"I think it's extremely important to keep sight of Tracy Latimer's humanity," Catherine Frazee, a member of the Council of Canadians with Disabilities, said outside the courtroom.
"In the midst of all these very technical legal arguments, it's so easy to lose sight of the fact that a child is dead and the man who killed her is still free," she said.
Marilynne Seguin, executive director of Dying with Dignity, a pro-euthanasia group, says another trial would only serve to "muddy the waters."
"The only fair, just decision that can be made at this point is to drop the proceedings and let everyone get on with their lives," she said.

Two cases with similar themes have emerged this year in Montreal. One involved a single mother who drowned her 6-year-old autistic daughter and the other a father who shot and killed his physically and mentally handicapped adult daughter and then himself.
